utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to proceed with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, we are, and that is Edin Suljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then, please, Mr. Usher, escort the witness into the courtroom. But what he -- that's what he understood already. While we are waiting until the witness arrives, I could inform the Defence that if there's any urgent need to have a smaller document translated, it can be offered to the Registry, to the services who provide the translation. But especially if there's -- if it has to be done urgent, for example, because we ordered that a translation should be there, then the best way of doing it is to attach to the request perhaps the page of the transcript in which the Chamber ordered that a translation should be provided, and perhaps highlight in yellow the order. That, as far as I understand, could be of some assistance in order to get a quicker translation. But of course, only if it's a smaller document and not big ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence thanks your Chamber, Mr. President, for this. We were just about to do so. What we hadn't told you last time is that, as a general rule, if we go through the translations services of the Tribunal, the delays are very long, one month to three months, I believe. This is the reason for which we used a rough draft, but thanks to your assistance, we will rely upon it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, I assume. Mr. Suljic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you before you testify in this Court to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The usher will now hand out the text of this declaration to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, the order in this courtroom is that you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, then by counsel for the Defence. And whenever the Judges have any questions, they will put them to you as well. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Suljic. Could you please start by telling the Court your name and your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: My name is Suljic Edin. I am in charge of the legal services of Sipad, interior in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you're a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am a lawyer, and I graduated from a law school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the early 1990s, before the conflict started, were you engaged in any type of activity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I was also working as a lawyer in a firm in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at the beginning of the conflict in 1992, did you become engaged in any way related to that conflict?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992, to be more precise, in the month of June 1992, I was mobilised and I was drafted within the army of the ABiH. Up until that time, I had no function within the party or within a political association.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in this army?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In the army, I remained up until the month of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in September 1993, were you employed in another capacity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In September of 1993, I started working in what was called at the time the CSB, or the MUP as it is called today, of the Sarajevo department, canton of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this CSB, as it was called then, is or was the regular police force for Sarajevo, was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The CSB, the Security Services Centre, was an institution belonging to the state, and it also existed there before the war, and it continued being a security service centre during the war. And it operated under the same principles as it had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did you come to be employed there, and what was your appointment when you became appointed there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I was working in the crime scene department because a lot of people had left that department. Some posts became available, and the position of a crime scene inspector was available. I had found out about that job through a friend. I then made a written application. I forwarded it to the CSB, the Security Services Centre, and I suggested or I asked at the time I take what was called at the time a work obligation and that I work there for -- within the Security Services Centre. My first job was in the criminal department, breaking and entering and material damages. This is where I worked up until the month of January 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, this is where you worked up until when?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Up until the month of January 1994. This is when I was transferred in the second department. This department was called Department for War Crimes and Genocide. It was a department which was to investigate and to try crimes carried out during the war, and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain in that department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I worked in that department up until the month of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you are presently a lawyer with a company. Just tell us for how long did you remain with the police force, or when did you effectively leave the police force?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In the Security Services Centre, I worked from the month of September 1993 up until the month of May of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you remember the 5th of February, 1994, at about mid-day or after mid-day that day, where were you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The day before, i.e. on the 4th of February, 1994, according to my duty assignment, I was on duty at the CSB. And according to the regulations of the time, the man in charge, the duty officer, was beginning his shift at 4.00 p.m. and he was to take part in all the investigations that had to do with the department in which he was working. On that day, the shelling on the Markale market and the massacre of the Markale market occurred, and as a duty officer within that Department for War Crimes and Genocide, I was part of a team that was to carry out the on-site investigation. We had to gather all clues and elements involving the massacre in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, where were you when you learned about this event at Markale market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I was in the offices of the SCB -- CSB, rather, which were in Marin Dvor. That was in the central part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about what time did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely. I know that it was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was on the 5th of February, 1994, was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were part of a team involved in the investigation. Did that team leave from the police building and go to the market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: From the police building, the whole team left without the investigating judge, who we picked up on our way there. We went to the courthouse, and together with the investigating magistrate, we arrived on site. I don't know how long it took exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly tell us what were your observations when you arrived on the scene of the market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: On site, when we arrived, we found traces of blood, scattered objects that were on the stalls, human body parts, as well as a great number of citizens that were in a state of panic. And they watched the scene in terror. The site was already secured. The police had proceeded to do that, police from the Stari Grad Police Station. And on site of the Markale market, it was not possible to approach that perimeter. Nobody had access to it aside from us, who had come there to carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there ballistic specialists with your team?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Every time that we do an on-site investigation, the team -- the team would be comprised of ballistic experts, crime scene technicians. There was always a photographer, as well as a representative of the services for the investigation of war crimes and genocide service within the CSB. And the on-site investigation was presided by the investigating judge, who on that day was on duty in the courthouse. This was the composition of the team, of our team, and such a team came out to carry out the on-site investigation on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after investigations were conducted at the site on the 5th of February, 1994, did you go anywhere in particular in respect to the continuing investigations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After conducting the on-site investigation, I went to the Kosevo Hospital in order to establish the identity of the deceased and of the wounded people, people who had died therefore and were wounded as a result of this massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that your primary role in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The war crimes and genocide division played a certain role in such investigations. The role was to determine the identity of the injured and those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, what did you do in respect to this task of trying to identify the dead and the injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In the admissions department of the Kosevo Hospital, the records are kept of all the persons who had -- had been admitted to the hospital, so the full name of the person admitted is recorded, the time of admission, as well as other personal details. And these records enabled me to determine the number of patients that had been admitted to the Kosevo Hospital in the time period after the explosion at the Markale market. After that, I went to the morgue and there, on the basis of the documents that I had gathered from the personnel in the morgue, I verified the identity of the persons who had been killed and brought there after the explosion at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you interview any persons in respect to your determination that these persons had been killed at the market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The duty personnel in the Kosevo Hospital at the admissions and also in the morgue, and they told me that all the patients that had been admitted were, in fact, the people who had been killed at the Markale market. And their knowledge is based on their conversation with the people who had brought in the dead and the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in attempt -- in attempting to identify some of these deceased and wounded persons, did you speak with friends and relatives of these people?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. For some of the deceased, we were unable to determine their identity because they did not have any personal documents or IDs with them which would make it possible for us to determine their actual identity. And that is why we asked the local radio station to notify the citizens, instructing them that if some of their relatives had gone missing or had not returned home on that day, that they should go to the Kosevo Hospital to see if they can identify any of the dead persons who were there in the morgue of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, during your investigations, did you -- can you tell us what was the composition of the persons who were injured at the hospital and those who were deceased at the morgue in terms of their ages, if you could give us an approximation.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were mostly elderly men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the Kosevo Hospital on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: On that day, I remained there for two hours, about two hours in the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, from your observations of all these dead, wounded persons, and the reactions of their family, how, if at all, would you say that this has affected you in respect to what happened to these persons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, the scene was frightening, terrifying, I mean the one in the morgue. There were four or five rooms there, and on the floor, there were about 60 dead bodies. Most of them were disfigured with shrapnel, the shell fragments. And each person who came there to identify a relative of his or hers, I would go through the morgue hoping, sincerely hoping, that that person would not be able to recognise any of his relatives. And this was particularly harrowing when that person was a friend of mine or a person I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next day, did you return to the scene at Markale?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, we went to the site again at the Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the next day, did you also return to the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the Kosevo Hospital again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which one did you go to first on the 6th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: We went to the Markale market. The scene was secured by the Stari Grad Police Station officers just as it was the day before, and the ballistic experts and the forensic technicians or the crime scene technicians were conducting their activities. And then I went to the Kosevo Hospital again in order --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You went to the Kosevo Hospital in order to do what, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In order to collate the lists of the victims that were changing from day to day with the new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And perhaps you could explain that a little bit further. Explain what you mean by collating the list of victims with the new information.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: On the first day, we had records of a certain number of the dead and a list of the wounded persons who were killed or wounded at the Markale market. A certain number of persons died due to their wounds the next day, so this information changed, and that is why I had to update the list to reflect the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were all of the injured and deceased taken to the Kosevo Hospital or were some of them taken to other hospitals?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The majority of the dead and wounded were taken to the Kosevo Hospital. A smaller number was taken to the French hospital, as it was known at the time, and some of the wounded were taken by the UN to their clinic which was located in the premises of the PTT Inzenjering in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which hospital is it that you call the "French hospital"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Before the war, this hospital was called a military hospital. Later on, its name was changed into the "French hospital." It changed its name several times so that I don't recall what its name was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on the 6th of February, 1994, did you observe any proceedings carried out on the bodies of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: All the persons who had been killed were examined by the pathologist, and he carried out an expert examination of the bodies in order to determine the cause of death. And every person that was brought into the Kosevo Hospital, the cause of death was determined and records were kept of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you present when these examinations were conducted?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I was present in most of the cases but I don't remember whether I was present during the examinations of all those who had been killed. But I had the relevant documents by the pathologist confirming the cause of death for all those persons, specifying that they were all killed by shell shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak -- or maybe I should ask this question first: What was the name of the pathologist? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The postmortems were conducted by Dr. Ilijas Dobraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you speak with him after he conducted these examinations or during these examinations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I spoke with the doctor about these autopsies, and Dr. Dobraca also participated in the process of identifying the persons because many of the citizens were, in fact, unable to recognise their relatives. And then certain information such as previous surgeries that they told Dr. Dobraca about were used -- this information was used to identify their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did Dr. Dobraca confirm to you anything in respect to the cause of death of these persons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. For every dead and wounded person, Dr. Dobraca would verify that the death was caused by mortar shell fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many days did you visit at the Kosevo Hospital in respect to your investigations as to the number and identity of the injured and deceased?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think that I went there for at least three or four days, but possibly even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to your investigations of the incident, did yourself and the police at the CSB Sarajevo prepare a report?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every service had to draft their section of the report that pertained exclusively to the areas in their jurisdiction. So I had the report of the ballistics expert, the report of the forensic technician, the crime scene technician, a photo file that was compiled by the photographer, and we also had the documents and the correspondence from the military hospital and the UN, confirming the death and injuries of those persons -- the victims. And on the basis of these reports, the genocide section compiled the final report which was then submitted to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let me go back. Yourself and the police were involved in the investigations, prepared a report which you signed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the system which obtained then in Sarajevo in respect to incidents like this, was another report done in respect to charges to be brought?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: According to the procedure, the rules of procedure, after all the elements have been determined and when they are stated in the report that we drafted, the criminal report is then drafted against persons known or unknown who committed the crime. And then this criminal report is then submitted to the chief of the CSB for his signature; and once he has signed the criminal report, the proceedings involving this criminal offence begin, the prosecution begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to the incident of the 5th of February at Markale, who prepared the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I took part in the drafting of the criminal report, and so did Nedim Curevac, a colleague of mine, also an inspector, and Nurija Makas, who was a senior colleague of ours, also an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the CSB who signed it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At that time, the chief of the CSB was Munir Alibabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, I respectfully ask to tender to the witness Exhibit P2365, and to also tender to the Court copies of it with Exhibit P2365.1, which is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Suljic, I'd like to take you to the page of that document with the number 0026-8323 at the bottom of the page. Do you see a copy of your signature there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the document was also signed by the colleagues you mentioned earlier, Nedim Curevac and Munir Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is a police report of the incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly to go through the document - I'll not ask you about every word on it - the first page marked 0026-8315 is a cover page summary of the event?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I, if you will, take you to the page marked 0026-8319 at the bottom of it. Now, that is where the actual police report that you drafted with your colleague begins. Can I ask you who from your report were the ballistic experts present at the scene on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The ballistic experts were Cavcic Hamdija, Mirza Sabljica, as it says here in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the second page of this report, you have a reference indicating that it was established that the projectile was launched from a north north-eastern direction.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was that information obtained from the ballistic experts?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this information was gathered by the ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the penultimate page of the report, you speak of interviews with citizens who are located -- who had been situated on the flight path of the shell that exploded at Markale market. Can you see where you have made that reference?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Our role was to find all the circumstances and establish the circumstances and find all the facts that are pertinent to this incident. This is why we conducted interviews with a certain number of injured citizens who, through their statements, confirmed the time and place and the way the people were injured. So we gathered those statements, and we use them as proof later on at the stage of the criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to take you back precisely to the area I was referring to. You said in this report, and it's the page before the last, that interviews were conducted with citizens on the flight path of the shell. Was this flight path as it had been -- or should I ask, the flight path that you refer to, the path that had been determined by the ballistics experts, that is, to the north north-east?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The information was received from the ballistics expert, who was able to determine from which direction the projectile was fired. In this case, we're talking of a shell. This is why we tried through interviews with citizens who were there on the flight path to establish the fact whether they may have, perhaps, heard at the time of the incident the explosion or the detonation or if they had heard the shell flying over which, through the findings of the ballistics' experts, would have flown over their houses or their dwellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have a look at the third page, I think it is, of the report -- I think, on your copy, it's the second page, on the original copy, the second page. From your report, is it correct that on the 6th of February, there were three court experts who attended to participate in the investigation? And I invite you to have a look specifically at the persons at number 7, 8, and 9 on the list of that page.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The following day, during the on-site investigation, the following experts were present. They had a greater experience and they had better training in that field, which was important in order to find out the direction from which the projectile was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. On the third page of the report -- may I just confirm if that is the third page on your report. The fourth page of your report, the page numbered 0026-8322, there is a summary of the numbers of deceased and injured persons. From your investigations, the summary indicates that there were 142 people who incurred minor or serious injuries that were admitted to the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the information that we can see in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the shell claimed 67 lives?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the report, it is indicated that Kosevo Hospital admitted 167 victims, of whom 106 suffered minor and serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the state hospital had 31 admitted who suffered minor or serious injuries but did not die?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the French battalion hospital had 8 victims; 7 of them who suffered serious injuries and were admitted there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is 106, 31, and 7, which is 144. There is a slight difference between the number you had above at 142 and the total 144. Could you just briefly, if you could in a sentence or two, explain that.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It is probably a technical error. The official information -- informations are those that exist in the lists of deceased and injured. It is possible that there had been a mistake during the printing, the typing, of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You were personally involved in the investigations at the Kosevo Hospital where the vast majority of the casualties were taken to. Were other members of the police team involved in investigations at the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My colleagues were involved in the establishing of the identity people who were in the French hospital or what was known as the military hospital, and the UN hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there were also victims at the -- what is referred to here as the French battalion hospital.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The hospital of the French battalion is not, in fact, a UN hospital, and it was probably under the control of the French battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a UNPROFOR French battalion who were then based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to have a look at that page of your report numbered 0026-8321, from that report, can you confirm that they, at your request, provided a list of the dead and injured who were taken there in respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also, some of the victims of this incident were also evacuated to other countries?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the police prepared a list of the deceased and injured, and also a criminal report was also prepared by the police which was signed by one Mr. Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your leave, may I put to the witness Document P2366, and also tender to the Court that document and its attachment, P2366.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have looked at that document, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the pages marked 0026-8620, are those pages a computer print-out of the deceased from this incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the pages marked 0026-8623 to 8624, are they a part of a computer print-out of the list of injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand which pages you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the pages with these numbers at the bottom of the page: 0026-8623 and 0026-8624.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are part of this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who inputted the information into the computer? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, the computer operator was Goran Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the document -- the data from which these print-outs were made, was the data or was the inputting ongoing over a period of time or did it remain static, in that it was just put in the computer on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: This data was updated following information received by the hospital, and those informations would change all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have a look, if you will, at the page numbered 0026-8624. That is the last page of the list of deceased, and the number of the last person is number 151. I beg your pardon, that is the list of the injured at page 0026-8624. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court the difference, if you may, between this figure of 151 and the figure in your police report of 142 -- or 144, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The discrepancy probably occurred because at a later stage when we verified the information, we would not -- we were not able to confirm with certainty the identity of all the people on this list, or that they were injured, in fact, at the Markale market during that incident. This is why those people were eliminated from the list when we drafted the final list of injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I take you, then, to that part of the document which has on it at the bottom the numbers 0026-8627 to 0026-8634.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I apologise to the Court, perhaps in the course of this I should have been referring the Court to the pages on the English translation of this document because it's a pretty long document. The English translation is 0087-7805 to 0087-7810.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This part of the document which is headed "criminal charges," I invite your attention to the last page of it, 0026-8634.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's a signature there below the typewritten name Munir Alibabic. Is that the signature of your superior who signed it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time Alibabic was the chief, and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was this the final report or your last report with all your confirmed findings with respect to the dead and injured that you participated in writing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the last part of the report that we usually do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would the list of the dead and the injured in this report be, to the best of your knowledge, an accurate reflection of those that were killed or injured at Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an accurate reflection of those that were killed and injured, and it is the final list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I take you back to the computer-printed list which you said, in effect, was a work in progress, and I'd like you to look at the list of deceased -- I beg your pardon, the list of injured from 0026-8623 to 0026-8624.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the first page, that is 0026-8623, the list goes up to number 53. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the next page, it goes to 109 -- it starts, I beg your pardon, at 109.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the reason for this? Well, before we ask about that, I take it that it would mean that there's a page missing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The list is incomplete. I can just confirm this, and I can confirm to you with certainty that this list was made in the -- according to the normal order, and I think that this must have been a mistake during the photocopying process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it is your evidence that the final official list is that which was signed the document by Mr. Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, but we don't have the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I was just at a point to ask. It might be the same. Mr. Stamp, if you're referring to the page ending with the number 8623 and you say that the list goes up to number 53, that's true if you take the original one. If, however, if you would look at the translation, it seems that 623 and 624 have been interchanged. At least, if you look at the bottom, the reproduction of the numbers at the bottom of the list, you see that there's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, just to clarify the issue, was this the issue you wanted to raise, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your humble servant, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I think that -- it's now at least on the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we should place it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that we could note this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, it is 10.30. How much time would you still need approximately, which would enable me to decide when we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just about to move on to another area, which it probably would take around 10 to 15 minutes, so perhaps this might be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we might have the break now. But may I ask you, when you -- yes, well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If we take a break now, could we not perhaps ask the technicians to check the ventilation in this room because I am under the impression that we are all suffocating, and your humble servant, myself, the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be a consequence of the weekend where the usual systems do not function, but I'll ask Madam Registrar. Madam Registrar has taken whatever measures to have a better air-conditioning in this room, and it might be a matter of time until it becomes effective. May I then ask you just before having a break, Mr. Stamp, we have had several times questions about translations, et cetera. I just had a quick look, of course. I was not able to go through P2365 thoroughly. First of all, I noted that the translation is -- well, there are a few markings in it, but that would not cause me to make any observation. But going quickly through the text, would you please try to find with me page 0026-8321. That's the... Yes. In the original. Not in the translation but in the original. Would you look perhaps at the end of the first paragraph, fourth line from the bottom of that first paragraph, you may see that there's a sentence which starts with a word - and of course my pronunciation is not correct - "rekonstrukcija." Do you see that word? So first paragraph, the first line of the original of 8321. You found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't found it as yet. Is this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Is this on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The B/C/S original, the page ending 8321.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately at the middle of the page, that's where the paragraph ends. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the fourth line from the bottom of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you see a sentence starting with the word "rekonstrukcija."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I now see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look two lines lower, the sentence ends with "60 degrees plus or minus 5 degrees." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you perhaps please try to find during the pause in the translation of this page where the translation of this sentence appears? I recognise a few words in that sentence like "stabilizator" and "projektil," and I'm fully unable to find any translation of this sentence. But perhaps you check that during the break, and inform us after the break. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will verify, Mr. President, are you talking about the ERN number ending with 321, 8321?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I must say I do not see the words "rekonstrukcija" in the first paragraph. Mr. President, is this the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the document. But I think Mr. Stamp found it. Perhaps if you try to find it during the break as well, and we'll be informed by Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the fourth line from the bottom on the first. Yes. We'll have a break until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say welcome back in the sauna. I am informed that everything is done in order to bring the temperature down to an acceptable level. It was partly due to not changing the system from wintertime to summertime. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have in the time allotted made enquiries as to the reasons for the discrepancy in respect to the translations. We have not had any official explanation as yet from the responsible unit and I am told that we will have an explanation by the end of today or tomorrow. However, I am told that the probability is that the omission is the result of error, that this sentence was overlooked, and pending obtaining a full explanation because I will still follow it up, I propose to ask a question -- ask the witness to read this sentence into evidence, into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that it will just be one line. As least we will have a translation in the record which is, well, of course, not the ideal solution for the problem, but at least it helps us out for the moment. You will understand that the problem of the Chamber is, in general, that we would not be happy that we have to check every document for the accurateness of its translation. I mean, it has happened now several times in all different variations but I would not be amused by sitting at my desk every day and checking whether every part of the document is translated. That's our major concern. You may ask the witness to read that part so that at least we have a provisional translation in the transcript. Please proceed. Mr. Usher, would you please... Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence would like to point out that it is absolutely indispensable to do so as you said. There are already mistakes in terms of the landing, the degree. We are talking about from 45 degrees to 60 degrees, so the degree is already a mistake or there is a problem or a discrepancy, and this is very important for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least whether the content of the document is an error or is in contradiction with other parts of the evidence, that is, of course, a totally different matter. But at least we need to know what is there. Please, could you guide, escort the witness into the courtroom, Mr. Usher. Mr. Suljic, you are the only one who is not aware of what I just said about the technical problems and the temperature in this courtroom. Everything is done in order to bring it down so it is a more acceptable temperature in this courtroom. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, could you have a look at your original report, your police report, again at the page marked 0026-8321, and I think you have it on document -- Perhaps you could assist us, Mr. Usher. We are looking at P2365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it is in the hands of the registrar. I think it is the seventh page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is perhaps the page printed at the bottom 0026-8321.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the first paragraph of that page, and there is a sentence, next to last sentence of that page, which ends with the figure "5" and the figure designating degrees, "5 degrees." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there are two sentencing following each other, both having the same ending.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at the one that is the next to the last sentence of the paragraph that ends with "5 degrees." And there is a sentence which follows which is a last sentence of that paragraph. Can you say what word that sentence begins with?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: All the activities and all the evidence found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues...] Mr. Stamp, I don't quite follow you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I ask it, put it this way. I am afraid I was not -- I didn't feel confident to try to pronounce that word. Can you look at the sentence beginning with the "rekonstrukcija"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. "The reconstruction of the position of the flight stabilisers of the exploded projectile found on the -- in the asphalt surface led to the determination of the angle of descent of 60 degrees plus/minus 5 degrees."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, just for the record, Mr. President, may I just state that that sentence which the witness just read is a sentence which was not on the original translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This determination of the angle of descent was made after the analysis by the court-appointed experts that you mentioned before: Kurtovic, Zecevic and Hadziomerovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated to us that you interviewed various persons who lived or who were positioned on the path of the flight of the projectile as it had been indicated to you by the ballistic experts. Did they confirm the direction and the area from where the missile came?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at that page of your report which is now marked 0026-8322.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you have a look at the third and fourth paragraphs of that page.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These witnesses all confirm that the shell was launched from the direction of Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were reports of interviews with these persons done?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Suljic, take you back to the examination that you said were conducted by Dr. Dobraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I may, with your leave, Mr. President, have the witness -- have tendered to the witness this Document P3061. For the Court, it is P3061.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to quickly look through those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to check something, and I will be back in just a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here I am. Mr. President, just to take one example, and I hope that this will be the last time, but I just wanted to show you with this example, to show you how the Prosecution is playing a game with the Defence. I don't know how to call it. If I take 8694, Exhibit 8694, that you received, it is a perfectly legible document, Mr. President. I think that you will agree with me. And we have the document that was given to us bearing the same number, and this is the example -- this is the copy with which we had to work. We had a considerable amount of documents communicated to us by the Prosecution on the deliberate -- in a deliberately illegible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, make your point. And for the time being, I do not assume either party to intentionally try to obstruct the work of the other. So you are fully entitled to complain about illegible documents. But whether or not this was intentionally done, it would be rather stupid to at one moment provide you with a legible copy, and another moment with an illegible copy. But let's refrain at this document, until there's good ground to assume that there is a good basis for it, that it is all intentionally done in order to obstruct the other party. That is not my starting point. But if there are good grounds to believe that, then of course you may come back with that. But let's just for the time being first concentrate on what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. So I do say the following: I was not able to prepare the cross-examination with documents such as this one. We are talking about a black box. All the documents we received are in that state. I do not understand why was I delivered documents in such a state, and I was not able to prepare the defence of General Galic. And I do say this on a voluntary basis. When I say "voluntary," I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ask for better copies to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are constantly asking here, as general rule, that all the medical documents -- very well, Mr. President. I cannot spend all my time to say that all the documents I receive are badly copied, and I would like to have a clear copy. I may say it every morning when I wake up but it seems that it is falling into deaf ears. We have received translations of this document only this morning, and I would like to remind you that as a general principle - and I will repeat this every morning - that the Defence would like to get the original of these documents. On the one hand, we would be able to see what these documents are all about; and secondly, there wouldn't be a problem of a bad copy. And I am very astonished to see that with the number of document that are perfectly legible that were communicated to us today, not one is badly copied; whereas if I take any documents from the old documents that I received, if I just pick one out of the pile of documents, you will see that they are black boxes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to give you an example, first of all, I had -- I see that you are referring to a page where I have some -- still some difficulties to find. But let me say this, Mr. Piletta-Zanin: If you would have told us while making reference to a bad copy of a medical document which turns out not to be necessarily bad copy because there are better ones available, you would refer to that document, and you would have brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution owes you an explanation on why they did not provide you with the better-quality copy before, and that it has hindered you in preparing for cross-examination. I think we would have fully understood what we now understand, and that could have been done in three lines. And it would have been just as effective as what you did now. I think - of course, I haven't seen the originals, Mr. Stamp - but if this is true, that Mr. Piletta-Zanin has been provided the black box and only now gets a good copy, you owe him an explanation, and the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to raise another point, however, and the English translation - and I do sometimes like to work with the English translation - I must say that we only received it a few moments ago, first point. And the second point, Mr. President, for which we are asking the production of the original documents is the following: That if you look at 868 -- 8585 which I received, looking this way, it seems to confirm to me that the second copy, 268585, is the number, it appears that the date of the 5th of February, 1994 is very oddly clearer on the copy; whereas if I go to the second version, the more legible one, I must notice as well that this date is more legible, it is clearer, and I may allow myself to interpret it as if it was scratched out something on the paper, as if a date was added on. Only the production of the original documents would enable us to see what the case is. And this is why every morning, I will ask for the production of originals of this Chamber. But as a general comment, as I said the other day, "erga omnes urbi et orbi." I cannot say it differently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if we look at the page just indicated by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that is the one ending with 585, it seems as if there would have been once different characters in the originals. If you take it one page back, 8584, it also has the appearance of multiple entries, as far as the date is concerned. I think those are not the only ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence just wanted to confirm to you that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Inaudible. The interpreter didn't hear what Mr. Piletta-Zanin just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice, Mr. Stamp, that on all these documents where we find similar what seems to be redactions of original text. I really find it in many, many of them, that also in the copies where the date is mentioned, the copy shows far brighter, especially where the copies are relatively dark. You know that the Chamber can ask for authentication of documents, and you also know that we do not do it unless there is a good reason to do so. But I don't know whether you could given an explanation right now before we consider whether we will have to ask for authentication of these documents or that you first have to enquire further in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We had proposed to lead whatever evidence that this witness would give in respect to those documents. A great degree of what we can do in terms of calling witness is to explain whatever might be required to be explained, including the maker of the document, possibly, would depend on what is raised in issue by cross-examination and by the whole conduct of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the Defence, although it has not been formulated as an objection already against presenting this document, since it has the appearance of being a redacted document, I don't know whether -- of course, if the witness could tell us about it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not suggesting at all that this witness is in a position to do that. These are the documents as we have them in our position here. He can, to some degree, testify about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have to make a determination having regard to time constraints as to how many witnesses we call in respect to documents. These are decisions that, to a great extent, will have to be made having regard to the conduct of the proceedings, what is in issue, and primarily how much time we have to deal with every item which might arise. Because We could call witnesses to explain a variety of different issues which are raised, and it is a determination we will have to make in the course the trial. We have this witness here now, and he can say something about the documents, but not everything about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He did not make these documents and may I just -- I think I should be careful since he is here. And it is a decision that we will have to make whether or not we are going to call persons who made these documents or try to obtain the original of these documents. We have delivered these documents to the Defence on at least three occasions. We have sent copies to them. We were not aware up until now that they had some copies which were illegible. We have copies in our vault which they are always free to ask to have a look at; and any time they do so, we do facilitate them. Specifically in respect to the dates on the documents, if there is an issue in respect of the dates, we can make enquiries, and we can do as much as we can to satisfy the Court with explanations. But, of course, that will depend on the conduct of the trial, how much certain things become an issue. We can't call every witness that might be able to say something about every aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But on the other hand, Mr. Stamp, at first sight, it is one of the things that jumps to your eyes, that the dates are, well, not normal entries in these documents. But let me just confer with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Another reason that seems to be very important to us is, of course, it is absolutely impossible for the Defence, even if we are very willing to check dozens of translations that have just been delivered this very moment, we would like to work from these translations but we cannot. You will tell me it is the same form, it is the same document, but you have seen how it is important to make sure that there isn't one single sentence missing, and we cannot take that risk. And humanly, it is not possible for me to verify all these documents, to verify all the translations that figure in these documents at this very instant. On the one hand, we cannot work, we cannot prepare; and on the other hand, the originals are not produced, and it is quite obvious. So as you said, it would be best to just set aside these documents for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you might have noticed, as I have noticed, that these documents are forms with all the same content which, of course, we can check that, whether it is really literally the same. At least it has the appearance that apart from the form itself, that it's mainly the entries that are of importance, and the entries are dates, names and, usually in Latin, the diagnosis, which is abbreviated "DG" in the original documents. So I think that checking the -- yes. So I think as far as translation is concerned, that should not be the major problem in respect of this document as far as we, the Chamber, can see it now. Mr. Stamp, the Chamber has -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Regarding the translation, there won't be a problem as soon as Mr. Stamp will give us the translation of the stamp that appears on this document. Mr. Stamp, would you be able to give us the translation of the stamp that appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that your objection also concerns the stamp, and what we see at the translation, the stamp is mentioned but not literally translated. If you have any difficulty in this respect, I am certain that the additional translation of the stamp, if that is of specific interest for the Defence, will be easily be obtained. I see on some documents it is quite well readable. We see that it is both in Cyrillic and in -- and it's -- well, even 80 per cent could be translated by me already by now in that it's the faculty of medicine, that it is the University of Sarajevo and it is in Sarajevo. So let's not play games and let's concentrate on the really important aspects. Mr. Stamp, this Chamber decided that you may present the documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the witness, but the Chamber expects you to clarify the issue raised by Mr. Piletta-Zanin as to the entries, specifically, of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I am obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will depend on your explanation whether finally the documents will be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. May I make an enquiry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would the Court be satisfied with an explanation by myself or one of the counsel for the Prosecution from the bar or would the Court require a witness who could speak about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on the type of explanation. If you say we still have the originals here but we wiped it all out and put a nice date on it, then of course you could tell it ourselves. If it would be another explanation, perhaps it would be -- it could be done in what way, it is difficult to decide. Let's first try to find the explanation and we then see how the explanation can be brought to the attention of the Chamber. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will take the appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a very important point so I would like to raise it. I would like to examine the document 8585. This document is now legible. I have it now in the legible form, and it is very important that we see what is going on in this courtroom this very moment. I don't know if you can read underneath the inscription "05020" or "1994," rather. But I can just guess that there is a "3" there, maybe even a "9" under the inscription "994." I do not know if we have the same document before our eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number so that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 0026-8585.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] At the end. [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you look at the date, on my copy, finally in the copy that I can finally read, under "1995," slightly to the right, I can see that something appears to be "93" or it seems that it is the year 1993. I don't know if you can see it. I don't know if we have the same document. But on my document I can very clearly see that there is a "3" for sure, and may be in front of it a number "9."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that is what I pointed at before. That is exactly what I wanted an explanation about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but what I wanted to say is that, having received for this document, a document such as this one, Mr. President, I do not have the same number any more, but this is what I have received for this document, Mr. President. I would like you to look at it, please. I have it in my left hand. It is absolutely impossible that I work with this document, that I cannot discover elements that we see right now on this other document, and I must point this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I ask two things to the Prosecutor: First, I said that I think the Prosecution owes an explanation why they did not provide you with better copies before; and the second one is that we want a clarification, especially of these kind of issues. What you do at this moment is to repeat that it's intentionally done to deceive the Defence, that is at least what I -- but it is clear that these kind of things you could not, on the basis of these bad documents, you could not properly prepare whatever examination of these documents is concerned. So if, finally, you say you need more time, we will see that at the end of the cross-examination whether there are still issues left which you -- for which you need more time. We will see that at that very moment. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. In respect to the second question, the question of clarification on the dates, the Prosecution will endeavour to clarify the matter in a manner which pleases the Court and which is sufficient, hopefully, for my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the first matter as to the legibility of the copies received by the Defence and an explanation for that, these documents were served on the Defence on three occasions and this is the first occasion that we are becoming aware that they had illegible copies of these documents. If we did, we would have -- if we had that knowledge, we would have given to them the best copies we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that they have been served three times?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the second or the third time, were these better copies or still the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know which copies my friend refers to, which service. The point is, if I may, Mr. President, is that we did not become aware of legibility issues in respect of these particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to say that I am quite surprised and indeed quite concerned by this type of behaviour of my learned colleague who is presenting facts which are definitely not correct. I believe that my learned colleagues and we on the Defence team have had so many meetings where we discussed the documents, primarily medical documents, and we always lodged the same complaints, that the documents are illegible, cannot be read and we cannot accept this type of arguments presented to the Court. This was the reason why we always -- when I say "we," I mean we, the Defence, we always question the authenticity of the document. And now we are at the point, so many months after the beginning of the trial, that we are discussing the authenticity of these documents. I think that my learned colleague, Mr. Stamp, was present when I said that the Defence cannot do its work properly with the documents in this state, illegible as they are. So I am quite surprised to hear that this is the first time that the Defence lodged this type of objection. I think that I raised this issue of authenticity of the documents once before during the examination of one of the previous witnesses. This objection still stands, and if we receive this type of documents now, so many months after the beginning of the trial, I have to say that this raises quite a few concerns with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I was not present during the meetings between the Prosecution and the Defence so, of course, I cannot verify it, but I am quite unhappy that, first of all, that no better copies have been provided to the Defence. That be sure, since there are better copies available. That is apart from a creating problems for the Defence. I am not saying intentionally creating problems, but at least creating problems for the Defence. It is also a waste of paper and ink. So that is the first thing I am unhappy with. The second thing I am unhappy with is that it could not be solved, let me put it that way, and I am just at this moment not saying that the Chamber at this very moment would not be able, is not willing to pay too much time on that, who is to blame that the problem could not be solved. I also do understand that if you get a lot of bad copies that you start hating yourself if every morning, when getting up, you have to complain about bad copies. Nevertheless, if there is any problem with illegibility of documents that appear on the list of documents that will be tendered, I want the Defence - that is the only way the Chamber can deal with it - I want the Defence to inform the Court within 48 hours after they received a new list and the potential exhibits, whether there is any problem with illegibility of the documents appearing on that list. That at least enables us to send you back to the meeting room and solve the problem and not spend half an hour on it in court. So, therefore, the Chamber has full understanding for your position as Defence, but the Chamber wants to promote other ways of solving these kind of problems than to spend a lot of time in court on it. So, therefore, within 48 hours, from the new list, any illegible documents to be reported. Yes. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you have had a long opportunity to peruse those documents, Mr. Suljic. The documents numbers 0026-8534 to 0026-8596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. At this stage, I must make another observation which is the consequence of the partial or total illegibility of these documents. The Defence deems that when documents are notified or served on us and we cannot read them, they are not prepared according to Article 65 ter. So there is an objection to the communication of documents when it comes to communicate documents in black and white with which we cannot see anything, that is not to carry out its obligation of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, are the documents 0026-8534 to 0026-8596 copies of post-mortem reports signed by Dr. Dobraca?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, could you look at the document with the numbers ending 6861. I beg your pardon, 0026-8561. Have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see a stamp on it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please read, if you can, the words in that stamp or of that stamp.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina University of Sarajevo medical school, Sarajevo. It is written both in the Cyrillic and in the Roman script.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you -- did you compare the names on these documents to the names on your list of deceased from the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: When we were drafting our report about the incidents at the Markale market --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We can get to that later. Just if you could, could we deal with this specific end of it, and we can move on to whatever you were saying. Did you compare these post-mortem reports and the names on them to the names on the list of deceased from the Markale market incident of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At the time of the drafting of the report, we did not have these documents. We looked at the protocol which was done by the chair for forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. At any time, did you compare the names, any time at all, did you compare the names on these post-mortem reports with the names on the list of deceased from the Markale market incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the document numbered 0026-8537.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that name on this document, Azem Huric, one of the names on the list of the deceased from the Markale market incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember all the names from the list of those killed, and I stand by the report that I had done at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am not quite certain if I got the right document number. Would Mr. Stamp be kind enough to give us the information regarding this -- what is the document number. I can read 6853, but apparently numbers that are missing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 8537, didn't you say, Mr. Stamp? In the transcript, the last digit is missing. 537, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, are you looking at the document 0026-8537?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say if that name appeared on the list of deceased and injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to give me the list, the list of the dead and injured, before I can give you my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could, please, Exhibit P2366 be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would ask you, Mr. Suljic, to look at the final criminal report, which is -- on which the list of dead and injured are 0087 -- I beg your pardon, 0026-8628 to 0026-8629. Can you tell us now whether or not that name appears on your list of deceased?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No, this name is not on the list of the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, may I be allowed to ask the witness to take a pen and put a mark across that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. This is an example of what the Defence was not able to do, and must do at the last minute. We were talking about the Document 8537, so if we talk about this document, I must note the following, under item 2, in the original language, we can read as follows: [B/S/C phrase]. We have right in front of it, in the space to be completed, we can see elements that are legible which correspond to the examination date, whereas in the space to be completed, we see them. But we only see them in the translation that you have which is produced under the number 877721. So we can see that there is absolutely nothing in front of the examination date and autopsy date, whereas it is perfectly legible in the original document ending by the numbers 537, that there is a date, a date does appear and the date is there. Whereas in the translation, nothing appears. So even if every time we have a typical form which is true, we must have information that we can examine on every document. I am saying this because, not having had this information in its translated form, we see that the translation, the original date exists. We cannot ask the question of the witness. On top of it, we see a date which is 1994. It might be 1995. I am talking about the examination date, of course. But in one case, like in the other, it all seems more and more strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, looking to document, last three digits 537, it appears that apart from on item 3, also on item 2, which asks for a date, some explanation is needed as to the entry which is there or has been there or seems to be there. So I think that we when we are talking about dates on the documents, it is not just in line three but in line two. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you take a blue pen and put a line across that document 0026853?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so that the Defence may at least try to prepare, would Mr. Stamp be able to give us now the information pertinent to this document. The Defence is willing to make the effort, but we have to know what is the information. Is Mr. Stamp able to give us the information right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Stamp would have an explanation, I think I asked him for it. I asked whether he could give it right away or not. Is that the same for the document last three digits 537? C.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
