utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so may we take a break, ask Mr. Stamp to peruse through his file to figure out what is going on exactly, because we are taken back by this and we were not able to prepare fully. We cannot work this way. We cannot cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll take care that you will have an opportunity before starting cross-examination of the witness. So that you are able either to put additional questions to Mr. Stamp -- let's now proceed with the examination of the witness. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you put a line across it, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, apart from that document, do the other post-mortem reports reflect names which are on your list of deceased from the Markale market incident of 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So there are 62 post-mortem reports that you have in respect to deceased persons from the Markale market incident of 1994? That is 0026-8534 to 0026-8596, which would be 63, and there is one which is not relevant. It would be 62.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that these documents were not available at the time when you did your report on the 17th of February, 1994. Could you have a look at the date of the document which is towards the top left-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You are looking at the document 0026-8534, are you? Please, look at that one.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On that post-mortem report, the date is the 10th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One or two questions on a different issue. In your original report, you said that tail-fin and fragments of a mortar shell were found on the scene of Markale market? I am sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if during the war, while you were a crime inspector of police, lab reports or lab analysis were done on these fragments?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember no lab analysis were done because there was no lab in the wartime conditions. I don't recall having seen any lab reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just in case -- this is not on the record -- is it correct to say that the document, the criminal report signed by Munir Alibabic is a confirmed report with the numbers, names and addresses of the casualties of the Markale market incident of 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the final report and it verifies the actual state of the affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have no further questions in examination-in-chief. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I promised the Defence that they would have an opportunity at least during the break to the extent possible to prepare for cross-examination, we will have a break now until five minutes -- 25 minutes to 1.00, so that -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that this will not be necessary. It is not possible to read in detail these documents in just a few minutes. And I think that the witness should come back tomorrow because the Defence is definitely not ready, and will not be ready after the break either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The testimony in chief, I would say for some 70 per cent, was not about the documents. Could the Defence not start to cross-examine the witness and we will see where it ends? If we come at a point where you could not proceed, then, of course, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Mr. President. This suggestion is welcome. The Defence of course, wishes to tell you that after the examination of these documents, if we wish to re-examine this witness, we would like to have the possibility to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then have a break until 12.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pilipovic, I usually ask if the Defence is ready to cross-examine the witness, but I will change my question slightly and say, is the Defence ready to start the cross-examination of the witness? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the Defence is ready to start with the cross-examination, but we expect you to show your usual understanding and to allow us, both myself and my colleague, to complete the cross-examination. That is, for my colleague to complete the examination after we have studied documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm to us that on the 29th of November, 2001, and on the 3rd of December, 2001, you gave a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't in the year 2001. I didn't give any statements on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you gave statements to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was in year 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When in 2002?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was perhaps in late February, early March.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, when you say "late February, early March," you're referring to the year 2002, so that would be this time period?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has a statement that has been disclosed to the Defence by our learned colleagues of the Prosecution. The statement is dated 29th of November, 2001 and the 3rd of December, 2001. We would like to show this statement to the witness and we would like to get an answer from this witness whether it is right that he gave a statement in 2001 or in 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be shown the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the statement is in the English language, and since it is signed, we know that the statement is signed in English but we do have also the translation. I would like to hand it to the usher so that he may show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You did show him the English-signed copy at this moment, or all the copies?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, Your Honours, we have shown the statement in English. There is a signature on the front page, and also the personal details of the witness. I would now like the witness to state whether this is indeed his signature or whether this is the statement that he gave.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I do apologise. This is my statement, and the dates on the statement are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm to us that you did give a statement on the 29th of November, 2001, and on the 3rd December, 2001?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you had given a statement in late February 2002 and in early March 2002, can you please tell us, did you also sign any statements on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I was talking about this statement. But since I live life on the fast lane and I lost track of time, and I wasn't really thinking about the correct dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, when my learned colleague was asking questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, do you want the witness to read the statements or would you rather have them back at this moment? We usually do not have statements of the witnesses in front of them when being examined. So Mr. Usher, would you please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement is in English. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some lawyers do understand English; others do not. But I've got no idea --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to check with the witness whether he speaks English and whether he gave the statement in English or in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand English, and I gave my statement in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please confirm that the statement that you gave in, as you say, Bosnian language, that it was stated for the record in English and that you confirmed with your signature that the information contained in the statement that we have shown you are indeed correct, and that everything that you have said has been included in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Suljic, you told us today that you are working in -- that you work for the Sipad company?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, before the outbreak of the conflict, that is, before 1992, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I worked in a trading company called Sarajevo Promet. For a certain period of time, it was in fact a representative office of a firm in Belgrade, and later on it became an independent company with its seat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, when you told us that you worked in Sipad, can you please tell us, where did you start working for the Sipad company?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think that I started working for the Sipad company in 1998 or 1999. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, the reason why I ask you these questions is because in your statement that you gave to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, it is stated that your occupation is a lawyer and that before the outbreak of the war, that you were also a lawyer. Can you please clarify this? On the basis of which information is it stated here that you were a lawyer and you are a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, it was a mistake in interpretation, because when they asked me what my occupation, what my profession was, I said that I was a lawyer, that I had a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Suljic. Today, when my learned colleague asked you a question about your employment in the beginning of 1992, that is, at the time when the conflict broke out, you said that in June 1992, you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, when did the conflict break out in Sarajevo, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I do know that it began when the road blocks were set up in some parts of the city. That is when the first casualties occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with the Defence if we told us that it was in early March 1992 when the first casualties fell and when the first road blocks were put up in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The setting up of the road blocks in Sarajevo and the beginning of the outbreak of the conflict in Sarajevo, do you connect it any way with the declaration of independence and the murder -- the killing of a person at a wedding, at a Serbian wedding at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I'm not and have been not been politically active at any time, so I can't give you an answer to your question because I do not have the appropriate information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in that period, in March, in Sarajevo, that the road blocks were put up after these events?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in March, or perhaps not. I'm not quite sure, but I do know that the road blocks were put up in Sarajevo sometime in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that in June 1992 you were mobilised, can you please tell us in which municipality you lived at the time and where did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you go to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I lived in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, and I reported to the regional staff of the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, where was the Territorial Defence staff where you went to respond to the call-up? I mean, the premises, where were they located? Where was the building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was in the settlement of Ciglane, which is in the city centre, municipality of Centar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what kind of premises were those of the Territorial Defence staff for that part of the city?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was a new building that had been built right before the war. I heard that, before the war, it was used by the Ministry of the Defence or for some similar purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us on what street it was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what the name of the street was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you cannot recall the name of the street at the time where the Territorial Defence staff was, can you tell us what the name of the street is now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think it's -- the name is Husref Redzic Street. I don't know whether that was the name before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what period of time the names of the streets in Sarajevo were changed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I don't know when the street names were changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you responded to the call-up, can you please tell us which organ called the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think that the mobilisation was proclaimed in June, but I don't know who proclaimed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you had reported to the Territorial Defence staff. Can you please tell us what formation within the Territorial Defence you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Right at the beginning, in the first two or three months, I was in the unit providing security to buildings and persons. And later on, I was transferred to the logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the first two or three months you were in the security, can you please tell us which buildings did you provide security to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: These were mostly regional staff buildings and facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the regional staff buildings or facilities, do you mean to say that there were some other premises where the regional staff was located?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No. That was the building where I reported for the call-up, and mostly we provided security to that building. We were at the reception desk and did tasks of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that after two or three months, you were tasked to join the logistics battalion, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, this logistics battalion, what formation as it a part of, what formation it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think it was in September 1992, that is when the brigades were established or setup. At that time, I was a member of the 3rd Motorised Brigade, and there was this logistics battalion which was a part of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So in September 1992, you, as a member of the logistics battalion of the 3rd Motorised Brigade, can you please tell us, where was the headquarters of the 3rd Motorised Brigade and where was the headquarters of the logistics battalion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Both the headquarters of the battalion and of the brigade were located in the part of the town called Stup, which belonged to the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that both the headquarters of the brigade and of the logistics battalion were in Stup. Can you please tell us how many battalions were there in the 3rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because the figure changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many soldiers were there in the 3rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of clothes did the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade wear? Did they have uniforms or what?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, we did not have any uniforms. And later on, some of the soldiers were issued uniforms that were made of some kind of fabric. I don't know what kind of fabric it was, but some of the soldiers were issued a type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that "some of the soldiers were issued uniforms," are you in fact confirming that the other members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade were soldiers that were not wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: A certain number of soldiers did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what kind of arms did the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade have? What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about armaments. I know that soldiers had Kalashnikov rifles and automatic rifles which were used before in the former JNA. As for any other types of armaments, I don't know what they were called. I'm just not very familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the army BiH, the 3rd Motorised Brigade, until December 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the Stup area where the 3rd Motorised Brigade was stationed, was an HVO unit named Kralj Tvrtko also stationed there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm whether the headquarters of the HVO unit named Kralj Tvrtko was located in the Alija Alijagic elementary school?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the members of the Kralj Tvrtko unit of the HVO that you confirmed was stationed in Stup, can you please confirm whether the unit commanded by Juka Prazina was also active in the Stup area?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that this unit did not have a permanent station -- was not permanently stationed on that line. They would come there occasionally if there were any major combat operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on that line, and by that I take it you mean the line of the 3rd Motorised Brigade, that there were major combat operations going on there on that line, and that on that occasions, the unit commanded by Juka Prazina would come in to help. Can you please tell us, the armed combat, who took part in it, and what was the line that you were referring to when you say that combat operations were going on there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I did not go to the line of where the fighting was going on, so I don't know what the lines were. But the fighting was going on between the army of BiH and the members of the Serbian armed forces, and the units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, how much time did you spend on the line, on the front line? When I say "the line," I mean your command post, the command post of the logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I was in the rear of the front lines, because we were providing supplies to the units on the line, and I did not go to the line itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the combat operations involving the two armies that you have just described for us, how often did they take place?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Shelling and sniping was an everyday occurrence. And as for the attacks or attempts to break through, to breach some of the lines, I think that they also occurred quite often, but I can't be more specific as to the time interval how often it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say attempts to breach the line, the front line, are you trying to tell us that the lines shifted, that their positions shifted as the result of the fighting between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, in the 3rd Motorised Brigade, you said that you were a member of the logistics battalion. But was there also a snipers' platoon which belonged to the 3rd Motorised Brigade, according to its establishment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what units were a part of the 3rd Motorised Brigade. I was -- my task was the medical service, to take care of the medical service, and of the quartermaster supplies for the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in general terms whether snipers' units were operating within brigades? Was there such a unit at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the 3rd Motorised Brigade had such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you don't know whether the 3rd Motorised Brigade had such a unit or not, do you have any knowledge of any such units existing as part of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I met some members of the BH army who had the sniper sights on their rifles, but I do not know whether they actually belonged to the snipers platoon or any other unit of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you would come across members of the BH army with sniper rifles, can you tell us whether they had any characteristic uniform, apart from the rifles that they had, which would immediately label them as members of a sniper unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think that they wore uniforms. I mostly came across them on the lines or in the area of operations of the 3rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you came across such people in the area of operations of the 3rd Motorised Brigade, can you please be more specific as to the actual positions and locations where you met them? Did they have their positions from which they were operating, did they have the snipers in placements, as they are called?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I never came across them in their -- on their positions, but mostly in the area where they had their meals and where they rested.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you came across them in the areas where they had their meals and where they rested, are you trying to tell us that the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade had their own kitchen where they had meals, and premises where they rested, their quarters?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in the area where the 3rd Motorised Brigade had its positions, which buildings are we talking about? Were there several buildings where the members of that unit took their meals and rested?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was just one building. It was the Elektro Privada, the electricity supply company building, which at the time was abandoned. It was an empty building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us on what street was this electricity supply building, in what part of the town, of the city?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was also in Stup, but I don't know the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, how much time would the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade spend on the positions, and was this Elektro Privada building in fact sort of a barracks where the soldiers were quartered?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time the soldiers would spend on the line. And in the basement of that building, they had the premises where they could sleep and take their meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So on that street where the Elektro Privada building was, the electricity supply company building was where the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade were located, were there any other buildings or locations where the members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade were located, apart from this building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that street where the Elektro Privada building is located, was the front line running through that street, the front line manned by the 3rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The front line ran in front of the Elektro Privada building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the front line ran in front of this building, can you please tell us how far away from each other were the positions of the two armies?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the front line went because it was not a straight line. But I do know that the first trenches were located approximately 200 metres away from the building where the soldiers were quartered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us -- you say that the trenches were 200 metres away from the building where the soldiers were staying. Can you please tell us how far away from the areas where the inhabitants of the city dwelled? How far away from these areas were the trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: There were no inhabitants there because it was the front line and there were no civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, where were the closest areas where civilians were located? In other words, how far were the civilian facilities and buildings away from the front line and the Elektro Privada building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 3rd Motorised Brigade were located in the part of town that was mainly an industrial area, and around the building where the headquarters of the 3rd Motorised Brigade was located, you had mainly commercial offices. And behind the electrical distribution building on the one side, at approximately maybe 1.000 metres, maybe more, you had apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was that settlement called where these apartment buildings were?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It was called Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us that on the line situated at a thousand metres from there, where Alipasino Polje was located, were there buildings where the logistics battalions were quartered, and the centre, the communications centre, of the 3rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Where they were stationed, I believe that the 3rd Motorised Brigade was quartered at Stup; whereas for the centres of the other brigades, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, when we talk about Alipasino Polje, what brigade had its positions on the area called Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that in the month of September 1993 you left the army of BiH and you started working in the CSB at the time, can you confirm to us that the CSB was operating within the Minister for the Interior Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The centre functioned within the Ministry of Interior Affairs at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when we talk about the Ministry of Interior of BiH, were there special units of the police that took part in the armed conflict during the period of the years of 1993, 1994, and 1995 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I do not know how the MUP at the republic level was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a special unit within the MUP called the Vikic unit which took part in the armed conflict in combat operations that -- which took place in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I do know that a unit under the command of Mr. Vikic existed, but I do not know which unit it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you told us that you do know that there was a special unit under Vikic, but you don't know under whom they worked exactly, could you tell us if members of the Vikic unit wore some special uniforms? And if so, could you tell us how they were armed as well.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with members of that unit, so I could not really give you an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if during the period of the armed conflict in Sarajevo, was there a special unit called Seva? It was a sniping unit.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I never heard about that unit during the war. I only heard about the existence of this unit after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that you only heard about the existence of this unit after the war, would you be able to indicate to us where you got this information? And do you also know where they operated, members of this unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: All the information linked to the existence of the unit called Seva I got through the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said that within the CSB, a department was created in order to investigate war crimes and genocide. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I do not know when this department was formed, but I know that in the month of January 1993, I was transferred from the breaking and entering department. I was transferred to this service which investigates war crimes and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that up until the month of January 1993, that is, as of the month of September 1993 up until the month of January, you worked for the department which investigated breaking and entering offences, can you tell us if during that period of time there were incidents of that sort, rather, breaking and entry incidents and also murders while you were working there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: There was a service for crime offences which took care of murders and other situations of the sort. But we took care of the breaking and entry that would have occurred on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When in the month of January 1994 you started working for that department, this war crimes department, can you tell us who -- which -- who created this department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who created this department.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After you started working there, were you told why this department was created? And if there was a special method of work and if you proceeded in a special way to establish war crimes, did you receive some instructions? Did you receive -- any explanations whatsoever as to the formation of this department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the department, I was given instructions. I was told what the inspector of such a department would do, and since those were different crimes, they are not just simple murders like in the other departments, they are not just crime-related offences and breaking and entering, as inspectors of that department, us inspectors, we were only to investigate that type of offences. We didn't have any particular powers; we didn't get any special instructions. We investigated crime the usual way like one investigates crimes in any other department of the police services and within the elements that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you started your work in the month of January of 1994. Would you be able to tell us what were the offences that you investigated as an inspector while you were working there in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: From what I can remember, I carried out an on-site investigation in Livanjska Street, where five children had died. I don't remember the exact date. Also, I also took part in a few on-site investigations where some civilians were killed from a sniping activity coming from Grbavica, and I also investigated some other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you investigated a few cases in which civilians were injured after a sniping incident. Can you tell us in what part of Sarajevo did that occur, and did you carry out an on-site investigation after those incidents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: On-site investigations were carried out mainly in the area of Marin Dvor, Pofalici. And also every time we carried out such an investigation, we made records of what went on. The team that took part in the on-site investigation proceeded and applied the methodology that exists already, that we knew of. And each inspector proceeded the usual way. We investigated according to our competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us names of casualties, of these victims, that died after the investigation you carried out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I could not tell you the names. I do not remember them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that a shelling incident took place in Livanjska Street where five children perished, can you tell us in what part of the city was this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: It's a settlement situated -- I don't really know exactly. Livanjska Street is at the end of the settlement. And I believe that we're talking about the settlement of Ciglane, or perhaps the beginning of -- actually, I believe that it's at the end of this settlement called Ciglane.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that it took part in the month of January.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell you what month it was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you to tell us about the month of January and to tell us if before you went out to carry out your on-site investigation regarding the Markale market incident, as an inspector of the department for the war crimes and genocide, did you also take part in on-site investigations regarding shelling? You also told us that you were a member of the team which was to protect civilians from sniping fire. Could you tell us if you were a member of a team in January as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of a team. I don't know which case we investigated at the time. But almost every shift was linked to one on-site investigation, if not more than one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that in the month of January, you went on a daily basis to carry out on-site investigations, can you tell us how many on-site investigations did you investigate? How many civilians died, and where did they occur?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The on-site investigations were carried out by the inspector who was on duty that day. And you were on duty twice a week approximately. While I was on duty, I also went to the premises. I could not remember now what on-site investigations I carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were on duty twice a week. Right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: The chief of the department was making the schedule, and he then was he was taking into account the number of inspectors that worked for that department. We would then change shifts. Another inspector was on duty the day after me, for instance. But if one of the inspectors was absent or if the shift was such, it would often happen that I was on duty twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who would give you an information telling you that a sniping incident took place or that there was a shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: During our normal day, up until 1600 hours, the information would come to us from our immediate superior, so the chief. And after those hours, after working hours, the inspector would receive the information from the on-duty operations officer who was on duty with regards to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who would give the information to the on-duty officer or to your superior? What is the name of the department that was transmitting the information, that was telling you that there was either a shelling incident or a sniping incident and that some civilians had perished in a certain part of town?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Within the CSB, there was the communications department, and that communications department was linked to all the police stations in town. And then the on-duty police officer would receive this information, and then he would get information from the CSB. And the CSB would receive this information and would further give it to the on-duty inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Those informations, did they come only orally or in writing, or how did you get it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot confirm to us that you would receive information in writing when it comes to information telling you that a civilian had perished after a shelling or a sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I would get the information from an immediate superior officer or from the on-duty officer. Now, I don't know where they got their information and how exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of February, 1994, you told us that you were on duty, so to speak. Can you tell us who informed you of the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Since this was an incident that took part while I was on duty, during normal working hours, I got the information from the chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us what time it was, what time of the day, and who made up the team that went out to carry out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: In the Department for War Crimes and Genocide, the chief of the department, aside from myself, who had to go out to the premises, he also told the Inspector Curevac, Nedim, to accompany me on site. And members of the other departments were chosen from their own chiefs. It's according to the schedule, according to the people who were on duty that day. And they were selected to go out and carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you told us that you and Mr. Nedim Curevac were there representing the service for the investigation of war crimes and genocide?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The other members of the team, who were they?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: They were appointed by their immediate superiors, and these were mainly inspectors who were on duty in their own services.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, how did you organise your work? Were you all in the same building? Did you go there together, to the site, to the scene?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At that time, all the departments of the criminal investigations division were located in another building separate from the building where the communications system and the crime scene technicians were located. I think that we came to the scene in two cars and that I, together with Nedim Curevac, had to go by the courthouse where the duty investigating judge waited for us. His name was Asim Kanlic. So the three of us went to the scene in one car, and the rest of the team was already there waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, that day, at what time did you receive this notification, and how far is your building from the scene, and how long it took you to get from the building to the market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was that we received the notification and when we arrived at the scene. But a certain period of time was necessary for us to consult each other, to see who was going to be there representing what service, and we also had to call the courthouse to check who the investigating judge was. Because after all, the investigating judges who were on duty were not actually sitting there in the courthouse, but they were staying in their own place, in their home, waiting for the call. So it took us a while to set up the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it took you some time to set up the team, how much time are we talking about, half an hour, an hour?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I think it was between half an hour and an hour. That's how much time it took us to prepare for the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you started the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that this information is noted down in the report. I can't tell you exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How much time had passed between the time when the incident actually took place until the time when you started with your investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I can't really tell you that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the weather like on that day, the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a nice, serene day, and the weather was nice.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the weather was nice, are you saying that it was sunny or what?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was sunny.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the scene, apart from your colleagues who, as you say, had come from the crime scene investigations section, were there any other people there at the scene, at the market itself?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: There were no people at the market itself. But the people were gathered around the market, around the Markale market. The market itself was secured by the police officers from the Stari Grad Police Station. There were also two or three members of the UN. They were also at the market, in addition to our personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm that you did find UN members there at the market. Can you please tell us, do you know if they were carrying out any kind of investigation on the site?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly why they were there, but in the course of the on-site investigation, UN members, representatives of the UN, took part in the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the team members, the technicians and the ballistics experts, who, as you say, arrived together with you and the investigating judge, do you know whether they carried out any procedures before the actual commencement of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: On that day, the on-site investigation was carried out. By that, I mean the determination of the facts and circumstances pertaining to the type of projectile, the direction from which the projectile had come, and members of the team who were tasked with providing ballistics expertise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and those in charge of gathering evidence at the crime scene also took part in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived at the scene, apart from the photographer, who you say was the member of -- a member of your team, were there any other TV crews filming the events? Did you find any members of the press there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: I can't really answer your question. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it that you don't know or is it that you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't really pay any attention to that, who was filming the scene and from where. Only the persons listed in the report were members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence would now like to stop, to make a break in our cross-examination, since our time is up. And with your kind permission, myself and my colleague will continue our cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Ms. Pilipovic. May I remind the Defence that -- well, let me put it a different way. There is a tendency that when the cross-examination is split up, that it takes more time than we would usually allow. That should not be a consequence of splitting up cross-examination. So therefore, the Prosecution took more time than they indicated before. Part of that was due to some -- well, I would say some procedural incidents, but not all of it. So I'll keep in mind whether there are any -- whether there will be any procedural incidents tomorrow. If not, I would say that another hour would be fair. If there are a few incidents, it might finally be one hour and 15 minutes, but that's the limit approximately the Defence should keep in mind. Mr. Suljic, we were not able to finish your examination today, so we'll continue tomorrow morning. We'll adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
